question: Former Labour Party peer, Peter Mandelson twice resigned from the UK Government under a cloud of corruption allegations before he was appointed European Commissioner for Trade in 2004.

In a statement on 3 February 2026, the UK’s Metropolitan Police commander Ella Marriott said: ‘Following the further release of millions of court documents in relation to Jeffrey Epstein by the United States Department of Justice, the Met (Metropolitan Police) received a number of reports into alleged misconduct in public office, including a referral from the UK government.

I can confirm that the Metropolitan police has now launched an investigation into a 72-yearold man, a former government minister, for misconduct in public office offences.’ In the light of the recent news of his divulging British state secrets and his close connections with paedophile millionaire Jeffrey Epstein: 1.
Will the Commission carry out a full and detailed investigation into Mandelson’s activities while he worked in Brussels as EU Trade Commissioner?
Will the Commission publish its findings in order to demonstrate a culture of transparency?
Will the Commission refer this matter for investigation by the Belgian police given the evidence of criminal behaviour by Peter Mandelson?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) Members of the College are subject to strict obligations arising directly under the Treaties as well as to the ethical obligations emanating from the Code of Conduct for the Members of the Commission1. The Commission is aware of the allegations against Peter Mandelson, who was Member of the Commission between November 2004 and October 2008.

It takes these allegations very seriously and has referred the matter for appropriate follow-up to the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), within the latter’s independent investigative function. OLAF has confirmed it has opened a case but is not in a position to share details on individual cases or probes beyond the information and data already made public.

This is in order to protect the confidentiality of investigations and of possible ensuing judicial proceedings, as well as to ensure respect for personal data and procedural rights. OLAF fully respects the presumption of innocence and the rights of defence of the persons/entities concerned. The investigation of other criminal offences remains the competence of national authorities.
